Neo4j

Source: vignettes/neo4j.Rmd
neo4j.Rmd

Use oauth_db_neo4j_api() to run Cypher queries with each Shiny visitor’s account. Neo4j validates their access token and applies the database roles mapped to that identity. Queries return data frames; graph objects stay in list columns. Install jsonlite alongside shinyOAuthDB. No database driver is needed.

This integration uses the HTTPS Query API v2. Self-managed servers need Neo4j Enterprise with SSO configured for JWT access tokens. Aura needs an SSO-enabled tier and configuration that accept the same user tokens at its database Query API. An Aura console login or management API credential alone does not establish that configuration.

Get the connection settings

Ask your database administrator for the database’s HTTPS Query API base URL and name, plus the identity provider’s issuer, required scopes and token audience. Use a maintained Neo4j 5.26 LTS patch or a newer supported release. Query API v2 starts with Neo4j 5.19. Self-managed versions before 5.25 must enable QUERY_API_ENDPOINTS in server.http_enabled_modules. Keep the server’s Bolt connector enabled: Neo4j uses it internally to execute Query API requests. Shiny only needs network access to the HTTPS endpoint.

For a self-managed server, the HTTPS port defaults to 7473. Aura uses HTTPS on port 443. Supply the base URL rather than the query endpoint:

graph <- oauth_db_neo4j_api(
  auth$connection,
  url = "https://graph.example.org:7473",
  database = "neo4j"
)

The client appends /db/neo4j/query/v2. Keep any reverse-proxy prefix in url. A neo4j+s:// or bolt:// URI is for a Bolt driver and cannot be used here. For a private certificate authority, pass its PEM bundle with ca_bundle.

Register the Shiny app

Register a web application with the provider trusted by Neo4j. Use http://localhost:8100 as the example’s redirect URI, then save these settings in .Renviron and restart R:

Setting Value
OAUTHDB_NEO4J_URL Database HTTPS base URL
OAUTHDB_NEO4J_DATABASE Database name, for example neo4j
OAUTHDB_NEO4J_ISSUER Provider’s HTTPS issuer URL
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID, OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET Shiny app’s OAuth registration

The example requests graph.read, which your provider must define or replace. Configure the audience to match the Neo4j OIDC provider. Some providers need an audience authorization parameter; pass that through the provider’s extra_auth_params. A scope name alone does not set the audience or grant Neo4j privileges. See Getting started for registration terminology and token settings.

A complete app

This example queries Person nodes. Replace the label, properties and scope with those used by your database. The user’s Neo4j roles must permit reading the selected nodes and properties.

After signing in, click Load rows. The app starts its workers once and stops them at shutdown.

pkgs <- c("shiny", "shinyOAuth", "shinyOAuthDB", "mirai", "jsonlite")
for (pkg in pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_NEO4J_ISSUER")
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "graph.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())
  graph <- oauth_db_neo4j_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_NEO4J_URL"),
    database = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_NEO4J_DATABASE", "neo4j"),
    required_scopes = "graph.read"
  )
  query_task <- oauth_db_task(graph)
  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke(
      "MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.country = $country RETURN p.name AS name, p.country AS country LIMIT 20",
      parameters = list(country = "NL")
    )
  })
  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*", onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)
    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at its registered redirect URI.

Open http://localhost:8100 in your regular browser to sign in.

Configure Neo4j SSO and permissions

Configure an OIDC authentication and authorization provider on Neo4j Enterprise. Set its discovery URL or explicit issuer and JWKS URL, expected audience, username claim and group-to-role mapping. The username claim should normally be the provider’s stable sub. Ensure the provider puts the groups needed for authorization in the access token.

For example, the administrator can map an identity-provider group to a Neo4j role. Grant that role access to the database and the relevant nodes and properties, and use different mappings when visitors should see different data. The Shiny app then runs the same query for every visitor; Neo4j controls the visible graph.

Use an access-token configuration. Some Neo4j SSO examples use ID tokens, but this client supplies only the visitor’s OAuth access token. Register the Shiny callback separately from any Neo4j Browser callback.

See Neo4j’s SSO integration settings and provider examples. For Aura, check the SSO availability and configuration for your tier and verify database query access with the intended user tokens.

Parameters, graph values and writes

Pass values separately from Cypher using a named list. Nested named lists become maps, and unnamed lists become arrays. Missing scalars and NULL become JSON null. Numeric values must be finite. To send a large integer exactly, pass a string and use toInteger($id) in Cypher; for dates and timestamps, use date($day) or datetime($at) with ISO strings or R Date/POSIXct values.

Project scalar properties for a table. Returning whole nodes, paths or relationships puts their native JSON values in list columns:

people <- graph$query(
  "MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.name = $name RETURN p, p.name AS name",
  parameters = list(name = "Alice")
)
people$p[[1L]]$properties

result <- graph$query(
  "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name AS name LIMIT 20",
  raw = TRUE
)
result$data$fields
result$data$values
result$notifications

raw = TRUE returns the parsed response and metadata after checking for query errors. It does not bypass authorization checks. Results use plain JSON: large JSON integers remain strings, while temporal, spatial and binary values keep the server’s string representation. Mixed values stay in list columns; empty or entirely null columns are logical because this format has no column schema. There is no automatic paging; bound large results in Cypher.

Use $execute() when you want the server’s update counters:

counters <- graph$execute(
  "CREATE (:Person {name: $name, country: $country})",
  parameters = list(name = "Alice", country = "NL")
)
counters$nodesCreated

Each call submits one statement in an auto-commit transaction. The client does not retain bookmarks or manage explicit multi-request transactions; queries use the server’s default routing and consistency behavior.

Token lifetime and failures

Create the client inside server(), then call it from render or reactive expressions. Each operation gets a current token. The client rejects a response if the authorization changes or loses required scopes while the request runs, and it cannot be reused in another Shiny session.

POST queries and writes never retry automatically, including after a 401. HTTP 202 can still contain a Neo4j query error, so the client checks the response body before returning rows or counters. A timeout or lost response does not establish whether a write committed. Check the database before resubmitting it, and discard saved results and bookmarks on sign-out or account changes.

The native integration check uses Neo4j 5.26.32 Enterprise with locally signed JWTs and real database roles. It covers database token validation, graph privileges and HTTPS; it does not establish browser sign-in, live provider key rotation, clustering or Aura compatibility.
